problemTypes.title: Tag, index and offset widths
recipe: Convert every size to a power of 2 in the addressable unit (byte or word).
Offset = log₂(block size); lines = cache size ÷ block size; sets = lines ÷ k.
Index = log₂(sets) (0 for fully associative); tag = address bits − index − offset.
problemTypes.trap: Using the number of lines instead of the number of sets for the index of a set-associative cache.

problemTypes.title: Average access time for one or two cache levels
recipe: Decide whether access is hierarchical (miss pays the upper level too) or simultaneous (miss pays only the level that answers).
Make every miss rate local: divide a global L2 miss rate by the L1 miss rate.
Apply AMAT = t₁ + m₁(t₂ + m₂·t_mem) for hierarchical, or weight each level's own time by the share of references it serves for simultaneous.
problemTypes.trap: Mixing a global L2 miss rate into the local formula, or adding t₁ to the miss path in a simultaneous system.

problemTypes.title: Tag-directory (tag memory) size
recipe: Compute the tag width from the address split.
Add the per-line status bits the question names: valid, dirty for write-back, and replacement bits.
Multiply by the number of lines (not sets).
problemTypes.trap: Forgetting the dirty bit of a write-back cache, or counting the data array as part of the directory.

problemTypes.title: Hit/miss trace of a block-address sequence
recipe: Turn each byte address into a block number ⌊a ÷ B⌋, then into a set number b mod S.
Keep one small list per set ordered by recency (LRU) or by load time (FIFO).
Mark H or M for each reference and count; the first reference to each block is always a compulsory miss.
problemTypes.trap: Mapping byte addresses straight to lines without dividing by the block size first.

problemTypes.title: Misses for a loop over an array
recipe: Write the address of A[i][j] in row-major order and the block it falls in.
Find which line each block maps to and how many rows of one column share a line.
If a block survives until its next use, count one miss per block; otherwise count one miss per access.
problemTypes.trap: Assuming column-wise traversal always misses: if the whole column fits without conflicts, it costs the same as row-wise.

problemTypes.title: Effective CPI from cache miss rates
recipe: Count memory accesses per instruction: one fetch plus the data references.
Stall cycles per instruction = accesses × miss rate × miss penalty (sum separately for instruction and data caches).
Effective CPI = base CPI + stall cycles; speed-up between two designs is the ratio of their CPIs at the same clock.
problemTypes.trap: Counting only data accesses and forgetting the instruction fetch every instruction makes.

problemTypes.title: Chips, decoders and address ranges in memory interfacing
recipe: Chips per row = target word width ÷ chip width; rows = target words ÷ chip words.
Every chip gets log₂(chip words) address lines; the remaining high-order bits drive a decoder that selects a row.
Row r spans addresses r·m to (r + 1)·m − 1.
Read the decoder enable: bits that must be 0 or 1 fix the base of the map; bits left unconnected (partial decoding) make each word answer at 2ᵘ addresses.
problemTypes.trap: Sizing the decoder by the chip count instead of the row count, or picking a chip from the decoder inputs while the enable bits disable it.

problemTypes.title: Read/write mix, line fill time and target hit ratio
recipe: Split references into reads and writes; under write-through every write pays a memory write, under write-back only dirty evictions do.
Compute the miss penalty from latency + line size ÷ bandwidth (or address + access + words × transfer for an interleaved memory).
Weight each class by its fraction; for a target time, solve the EMAT equation for h in the access model the question names.
problemTypes.trap: Charging writes only the cache time in a write-through cache, or mixing up hierarchical and simultaneous when solving for h.

questions.stem: A 32-bit byte-addressable machine has a 32 KB, 8-way set-associative cache with 32-byte blocks. How many bits wide is the tag?
questions.explanation: Offset = log₂ 32 = 5 bits. Lines = 32 KB ÷ 32 B = 1024, so sets = 1024 ÷ 8 = 128 and index = 7 bits. Tag = 32 − 7 − 5 = 20 bits.

questions.stem: L1 has a 1 ns hit time and a 10% miss rate. L2 has a 10 ns hit time and a 1% local miss rate. Main memory takes 100 ns. What is the average memory access time?
questions.explanation: AMAT = 1 + 0.10 × (10 + 0.01 × 100) = 1 + 0.10 × 11 = 2.1 ns. 2.0 ns drops the memory term; 3.0 ns treats the 1% as a global rate and adds it as a separate term; 11.0 ns charges L2 on every access.

questions.stem: A system has L1 (access time 2 ns, hit ratio 0.8), L2 (access time 10 ns, local hit ratio 0.9) and main memory (100 ns, always hits). Access is hierarchical: a request that misses at a level has already spent that level's access time before going down. What is the average access time in ns?
questions.explanation: Served by L1: 0.8 × 2 = 1.6. Served by L2: 0.2 × 0.9 = 0.18 of references, each costing 2 + 10 = 12 ns, giving 2.16. Served by memory: 0.2 × 0.1 = 0.02, each costing 2 + 10 + 100 = 112 ns, giving 2.24. Total = 1.6 + 2.16 + 2.24 = 6.0 ns. The same answer comes from t₁ + m₁(t₂ + m₂·t_m) = 2 + 0.2 × (10 + 0.1 × 100) = 6. Under simultaneous access it would be 1.6 + 0.18 × 10 + 0.02 × 100 = 5.4 ns.

questions.stem: Out of 1000 CPU memory references, 40 miss in L1 and 20 miss in L2. What are the local and the global miss rates of L2?
questions.explanation: Only the 40 L1 misses reach L2, so its local miss rate is 20 ÷ 40 = 0.5. The global miss rate divides by all references: 20 ÷ 1000 = 0.02, which equals 0.04 × 0.5. 0.04 is L1's miss rate.

questions.stem: A direct-mapped cache has 4 lines with 1-byte blocks and starts empty. The CPU reads byte addresses 0, 4, 8, 12, 0, 4, 8. How many hits and misses occur?
questions.explanation: Every address is a multiple of 4, so each maps to line a mod 4 = 0. Each reference replaces the block the previous one loaded, and no address repeats back to back, so all 7 references miss. 3 hits and 4 misses would be the result in a 4-line fully associative cache.

questions.stem: A cache holds 4 blocks, is 2-way set-associative with LRU replacement and starts empty. The CPU references main-memory block numbers 0, 4, 0, 4, 8, 0, 4 in that order. How many misses occur?
questions.explanation: There are 2 sets, and every block here is even, so all go to set 0, which holds 2 blocks. 0 M, 4 M, 0 H, 4 H. Block 8 misses and evicts the LRU block 0; then 0 misses and evicts 4; then 4 misses and evicts 8. Misses = 5. A direct-mapped cache with 4 lines would miss all 7 (all map to line 0); a fully associative LRU cache would miss only 3 (the compulsory misses).

questions.stem: A 32-bit byte-addressable machine has a 16 KB, 4-way set-associative write-back cache with 64-byte blocks. Each line stores its tag, one valid bit and one dirty bit, and no replacement bits. What is the total size of the tag directory in bits?
questions.explanation: Lines = 16 KB ÷ 64 B = 256; sets = 256 ÷ 4 = 64. Offset = 6, index = 6, tag = 32 − 6 − 6 = 20 bits. Each line stores 20 + 1 + 1 = 22 bits, so the directory holds 256 × 22 = 5632 bits.

questions.stem: A 1024-line, 4-way set-associative cache uses 20-bit tags. What comparison hardware does one lookup need?
options: 4 comparators of 20 bits and a 4-to-1 multiplexer
4 comparators of 28 bits and a 4-to-1 multiplexer
questions.explanation: The index selects one set, and the 4 tags of that set are compared with the address tag in parallel, so 4 comparators each as wide as the tag (20 bits). A 4-to-1 multiplexer then passes the data of the matching way. One comparator is the direct-mapped case; one per line is the fully associative case; the index bits are never compared.

questions.stem: Which of these statements about cache write policies are correct?
options: A write-back cache writes a block to memory only when it is evicted and its dirty bit is set.
With write-through, main memory holds the current value after every store.
No-write-allocate brings the block into the cache on a write miss.
Write-back produces one memory write for every store instruction.
questions.explanation: Write-back defers memory updates to eviction and skips clean blocks, which is why it cuts memory writes. Write-through updates memory on every store. No-write-allocate is the opposite of fetching on a write miss: it writes to memory and leaves the cache alone. One memory write per store describes write-through, not write-back.

questions.stem: An L2 cache is said to be inclusive of L1. What does that mean?
options: Every block present in L1 is also present in L2
Every block present in L2 is also present in L1
L1 and L2 never hold the same block
L1 and L2 are probed simultaneously
questions.explanation: Inclusion means L1's contents are a subset of L2's, so evicting a block from L2 forces it out of L1 too. The reverse cannot hold since L2 is larger; never holding the same block is the exclusive policy; probing both together is simultaneous access, an unrelated property.

questions.stem: Which statements about the three classes of cache misses are correct?
options: Raising associativity while keeping capacity fixed reduces conflict misses.
A fully associative cache has no conflict misses.
Doubling the cache size removes compulsory misses.
Increasing the block size always lowers the miss rate.
questions.explanation: Conflict misses arise from too many blocks competing for one set, so more ways per set reduce them, and with a single set they cannot occur. Compulsory misses are first references and happen at any cache size. Larger blocks cut compulsory misses at first, but with fixed capacity there are fewer lines, so conflict misses eventually rise.

questions.stem: With 4 frames, initially empty, the reference string is 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. How many faults do FIFO and LRU replacement incur?
questions.explanation: FIFO: 1, 2, 3, 4 fault (4); 1, 2 hit; 5 replaces 1, 1 replaces 2, 2 replaces 3, 3 replaces 4, 4 replaces 5, 5 replaces 1: 6 more, total 10. LRU: 4 cold faults; 1, 2 hit; 5 replaces 3; 1, 2 hit; 3 replaces 4; 4 replaces 5; 5 replaces 1: total 8. With 3 frames FIFO faults only 9 times, which is Belady's anomaly.

questions.stem: A processor has CPI 1.0 with a perfect cache. Every instruction is fetched from memory, and 30% of instructions also make one data access. The miss rate is 2% for all accesses and the miss penalty is 100 cycles. What is the effective CPI?
questions.explanation: Memory accesses per instruction = 1 fetch + 0.3 data = 1.3. Stall cycles per instruction = 1.3 × 0.02 × 100 = 2.6. Effective CPI = 1.0 + 2.6 = 3.6. Forgetting the instruction fetches gives 1.6.

questions.stem: int is 4 bytes and int A[64][64] is stored row-major starting at address 0. A 4 KB direct-mapped cache with 16-byte blocks starts empty. The program reads A[i][j] in the order for (j = 0; j < 64; j++) for (i = 0; i < 64; i++). How many cache misses occur?
questions.explanation: A[i][j] is at 256i + 4j, in block 16i + ⌊j/4⌋, which maps to line (16i + ⌊j/4⌋) mod 256. Rows i and i + 16 share a line, so the 64 elements of one column fall into only 16 lines, 4 rows per line. By the time the inner loop finishes, each line holds the block of the last of its 4 rows, so the next column (which needs the blocks of the earlier rows) misses again. Every one of the 4096 reads misses. Row-wise order would give 4096 ÷ 4 = 1024 misses, and so would this column order with a 16 KB cache.

questions.stem: A 16K × 8 memory is built from 1K × 4 RAM chips. How many chips are needed, and what decoder selects among the rows of chips?
questions.explanation: Two 4-bit chips side by side make an 8-bit word, and 16K ÷ 1K = 16 rows give the depth: 16 × 2 = 32 chips. Of the 14 address bits, 10 go to every chip and the top 4 drive a 4-to-16 decoder whose outputs are the row chip-selects. A 5-to-32 decoder would wrongly treat each chip as its own row.

questions.stem: An 8K-word memory is made of 8 modules of 1K words each. Which module holds word address 1234 (decimal) under low-order interleaving and under high-order interleaving?
questions.explanation: Low-order interleaving uses the 3 low address bits: 1234 mod 8 = 2. High-order interleaving uses the 3 high bits, i.e. which 1K block the address falls in: ⌊1234 ÷ 1024⌋ = 1.

questions.stem: A cache line holds 8 words. Main memory takes 1 cycle to receive an address, 20 cycles for a bank access and 1 cycle to transfer one word over a one-word bus. The memory has 8 banks with low-order interleaving, all accessed in parallel after the address is broadcast. How many cycles does one line fill take?
questions.explanation: The address is sent once (1 cycle), all 8 banks access their word in parallel (20 cycles), then the 8 words cross the bus one at a time (8 cycles): 1 + 20 + 8 = 29. From a single bank each word pays its own access: 1 + 8 × (20 + 1) = 169 cycles, so interleaving speeds the fill up by about 5.8. High-order interleaving would put all 8 consecutive words in one bank and also give 169.

questions.stem: A CPU has a 16-bit byte address bus. Four 2K × 8 RAM chips share A10–A0. A 2-to-4 decoder takes A12 (high input) and A11, and it is enabled only when A15 = A14 = A13 = 0; output r drives the chip select of chip r. Which statements are correct?
options: The four chips together occupy 0000H to 1FFFH.
If A15–A13 were left out of the enable logic, every byte of chip 0 would answer at 8 different addresses.
questions.explanation: Each chip covers 2K = 800H bytes, and A12 A11 = r selects chip r, so chip r spans r × 800H to r × 800H + 7FFH: chip 3 is 1800H–1FFFH and the four chips fill 0000H–1FFFH. 2800H is 0010 1000 0000 0000 in binary: A13 = 1 disables the decoder, so no chip answers; reading only A12 A11 = 01 gives the wrong choice of chip 1. Ignoring the 3 bits A15–A13 is partial decoding: each byte answers for all 2³ = 8 values of those bits.

questions.stem: A write-through, no-write-allocate cache has a 10 ns access time and main memory a 100 ns access time; there is no write buffer. 80% of references are reads and 20% writes. Reads hit with ratio 0.9, and a read miss is served hierarchically (cache probed first, then memory). Every write updates main memory. What is the average access time in ns?
questions.explanation: Read time = 10 + 0.1 × 100 = 20 ns. Each write costs a memory write, 100 ns, hit or miss. Average = 0.8 × 20 + 0.2 × 100 = 16 + 20 = 36 ns. Charging writes only the cache time gives 18; treating reads as simultaneous gives 0.8 × (9 + 10) + 20 = 35.2.

questions.stem: A cache with a 5 ns access time and a main memory with an 80 ns access time are probed simultaneously, and a reference takes whichever answers. What hit ratio gives an average access time of 12.5 ns?
questions.explanation: Simultaneous access: 5h + 80(1 − h) = 12.5, so 80 − 75h = 12.5 and h = 67.5 ÷ 75 = 0.9. Under hierarchical access the equation would be 5 + 80(1 − h) = 12.5, giving h = 0.90625.

questions.stem: A cache has 64-byte lines. Main memory has a 32 ns latency and a peak bandwidth of 1 GB/s (take 1 GB = 10⁹ bytes). How long, in ns, does it take to fetch one line from memory?
questions.explanation: 1 GB/s moves 10⁹ bytes in 10⁹ ns, one byte per ns, so the 64 bytes stream in 64 ns after the 32 ns latency: 32 + 64 = 96 ns. Paying the latency per byte, or forgetting it, are the usual slips.

questions.stem: A two-level memory has an 8 MB fast level costing 4 units per byte and a 56 MB slow level costing 1 unit per byte. What is the average cost per byte of the whole memory?
questions.explanation: Average cost = total cost ÷ total capacity = (8 × 4 + 56 × 1) ÷ 64 = 88 ÷ 64 = 1.375. 2.5 is the plain mean of the two prices; 3.625 swaps the capacities; 1.0 ignores the fast level.

pitfalls.text: The index counts sets, not lines: a 1024-line 4-way cache has 256 sets and an 8-bit index.
AMAT weights the miss penalty by the miss rate; hit time + miss penalty is the cost of one miss, not the average.
Hierarchical and simultaneous access give different answers on the same data (6.0 ns vs 5.4 ns in the two-level example); check which one the question describes.
A global L2 miss rate must be divided by the L1 miss rate before it goes into t₁ + m₁(t₂ + m₂·t_mem).
Pair write policies correctly: write-back goes with write-allocate, write-through with no-write-allocate, and only write-back needs a dirty bit.
A TLB miss is not a page fault: the page may be in memory and only the page-table walk is needed.
Divide a byte address by the block size before taking it mod the number of sets; mapping raw addresses to lines is only right for 1-byte blocks.
In a write-through cache without a write buffer every write costs a memory access, even on a hit: with 20% writes and t_m = 100 ns, writes alone add 20 ns to the average.

revisionCard.heading: Address split
lines: sets = lines ÷ k; index = log₂ sets (0 if fully associative)
tag directory = lines × (tag + valid + dirty + LRU bits)

revisionCard.heading: Access time
lines: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty
Hierarchical: t_c + (1 − h)t_m; simultaneous: h·t_c + (1 − h)t_m
Two levels: t₁ + m₁(t₂ + m₂·t_mem), m₂ local
Global L2 miss rate = m₁ × m₂
CPI = base + accesses/instr × miss rate × penalty
Line fill = latency + line size ÷ bandwidth; cost/bit = Σ cᵢSᵢ ÷ Σ Sᵢ

revisionCard.heading: Policies and misses
lines: LRU, FIFO (Belady's anomaly), optimal = farthest next use
3 Cs: compulsory, capacity, conflict (none in fully associative)

revisionCard.heading: Interfacing and VM
lines: M × N from m × n chips: (M/m)(N/n) chips, log₂(M/m)-to-(M/m) decoder
Partial decoding with u free address bits: 2ᵘ aliases per word
Low-order bank = a mod m; high-order bank = ⌊a ÷ (W/m)⌋

errata.claim: Q3: a 32-bit address with a 4-byte offset and an 8-bit index has a 20-bit tag.
errata.correction: The 20-bit tag needs a 4-bit offset (16-byte blocks). A 4-byte block would give a 2-bit offset and a 22-bit tag.

errata.claim: PYQ-3: with 4 frames on 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, LRU incurs 10 faults (FIFO also 10).
errata.correction: FIFO incurs 10 faults but LRU incurs 8: after the 4 cold faults, LRU faults only on 5, 3, 4 and 5.

errata.claim: PYQ-4: LRU with 4 frames on 1, 2, 3, 4, 2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 1, 2, 3, 7, 6, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 6 gives the classic count of 14 faults.
errata.correction: LRU with 4 frames gives 10 faults; 14 is the FIFO count for 4 frames.

errata.claim: PYQ-5: addresses 0, 4, 8, 12, 0, 4, 8 on a 4-line direct-mapped cache with 1-byte blocks give 6 misses and 1 hit.
errata.correction: All seven addresses map to line 0 and each evicts the previous block, so there are 7 misses and no hits.
